notes: Scratch refactoring (see references/preparatory-refactoring.md) intentionally has NO eval. Its trigger condition — you cannot see the structure by reading, so you must move code on a throwaway branch to learn — can't be honestly tested: a legible code excerpt destroys the trigger (the agent just reads it and tidies), and a 'design only' prompt forbids the editing the technique requires. Eliciting it would need genuinely tangled code (shared mutable state, temporal coupling, no nameable seams) that a strong agent can't read its way through — which we couldn't construct without a contrived strawman. Tidy-first IS eval'd (id 12, prep-refactor-tidy-first-or-eugene-cspt) because its passing behavior — recognize prep-refactoring is needed, plan the extraction before adding features — is observable in a design response. Do NOT add a scratch eval against regular-but-long code like employees_to_report; testing showed that's tidy-territory, not scratch. Shapes 13-14, the actions/calculations/data lens, and the immutability discipline are eval'd at ids 13-16. RED-phase baseline testing (Opus, no skill) showed a strong model already reaches good substance on all four scenarios — including the two don't-apply cases — so these discriminate on the reproducible FRAMEWORK (named shape, threshold gate, primitives-not-records, block-vs-Decorator, connascence, typed sig) and on false-positive resistance for the weaker models used in execute-plan subagents, NOT on raw outcome. They are regression guards in the same spirit as ids 6 and 11. Prompt wording note: ids 1-3 and 13-16 say 'follow its Review section' and ids 4 and 12 say 'work out the design before writing any code'. They previously named a 'Code Review Mode' and a numbered 'Stage 1 / Step 1 (Design)' from the old Quality Loop, which the shaping/delivery/review rewrite removed — the old names no longer resolved to anything in SKILL.md. Id 21 guards the deliberate removal of disable-model-invocation from execute-plan and brainstorm: both are model-invocable so the ambient skill can route into them, which means the shaping/delivery boundary now rests on the description negative triggers plus execute-plan's entry gate rather than on a frontmatter gate.

evals.name: shape-1-mode-dependent-field-in-pr-review
evals.prompt:
You are reviewing a pull request. Load the installed ruby-programming skill and follow its Review section.

PR Title: [TPF-1728] Configure sequential transmission delay

PR Description: Adds `min_seconds_between_sequential_transmissions` to `TransmissionConfiguration`, defaulting to `0`. Only used when `is_serially_transmitted` is true. NY keeps 90s delay, IRS/default gets 0.

Diff:
```ruby

  const :requires_separate_acknowledgement, T::Boolean
  const :client, T.class_of(Transmissions::BaseClient)
  const :is_serially_transmitted, T::Boolean

end
```

Review this code. What design concerns do you see?
evals.expected_behavior: The review MUST: (1) identify Shape 1 (mode-dependent fields) by name, (2) note that min_seconds_between_sequential_transmissions is meaningless when is_serially_transmitted is false, (3) check the threshold gate conditions, (4) propose an alternative design using Strategy or sum types (e.g., SerialTransmissionConfig vs ParallelTransmissionConfig), (5) ask the forward question about what happens when a new variant appears. The review should NOT just dismiss this as a minor concern — it should name the pattern and set a trip wire for when the split becomes mandatory.
evals.eval_result: Claude Opus 5 fresh-context pass (sandboxed re-run): named Shape 1, showed the invalid construction that type-checks, checked the gate, declined to force a split on one field, set the tripwire for the second serial-only knob, and identified Connascence of Value between the fallback and the struct default. An earlier unsandboxed run was discarded: the agent found the evolved version of this code in the zenpayroll working directory and reviewed that instead of the snapshot.

evals.name: shape-12-complex-boolean-logic-recognition
evals.prompt:
You are reviewing code. Load the installed ruby-programming skill and follow its Review section.

A teammate asks you to review this method:

```ruby

  company.has_employees? &&
    filing.period_closed? &&
    filing.state_code == "CA" &&
    (filing.wages_changed? || filing.withholding_changed?) &&
    (filing.total_difference.abs > BigDecimal("0.05")) &&

end
```

This method is also partially duplicated in two other places — one checks the same conditions but for NY instead of CA, and another checks similar conditions for federal filings with different thresholds.

What design feedback would you give?
evals.expected_behavior: The review MUST: (1) identify Shape 12 (complex boolean logic / Specification pattern) by name, (2) check the threshold gate (3+ conditions combined, same conditions reused across places, individual rules have domain names), (3) recommend extracting individual specifications (HasEmployees, PeriodClosed, InState, ValuesChanged, ExceedsThreshold, NotAlreadyAmended) as composable objects, (4) note the duplication across CA/NY/federal as a signal that extraction would reduce it. Should NOT recommend extracting if the boolean logic is simple or single-use.
evals.eval_result: Claude Opus 5 fresh-context pass: named Shape 12, checked all three gates, proposed named specification objects, and split CA/NY (real duplication) from federal (different axis of change), recommending a shared rule vocabulary rather than one parameterized composition.

```ruby
  when :electronic then "XML"
```

evals.name: strategy-pattern-from-spec-with-known-future-variant
evals.prompt:
You are starting implementation work on a feature. Load the installed ruby-programming skill and work out the design before writing any code.

Here is the spec:

---

## Background

Pufferfish's AutomaticWorkflowTransmitter currently supports sequential transmission via `SequentialTransmissionWorker`. NYS-1 filings use this with a 90-second delay between filing groups to comply with NY DTF rate limits.

The system has a `TransmissionConfiguration` T::Struct with:
- `requires_separate_acknowledgement: T::Boolean`
- `client: T.class_of(BaseClient)`
- `is_serially_transmitted: T::Boolean`
- `min_seconds_between_sequential_transmissions: Integer` (default: 0, only used when serial)

## Requirements

1. **IRS MeF (ship now)**: IRS requires sequential transmission like NY, but with only 2 seconds between groups instead of 90. The existing `SequentialTransmissionWorker` already supports configurable timing via `min_seconds_between_sequential_transmissions`. Wire up IRS MeF to use it with `min_seconds_between_sequential_transmissions: 2`.

2. **MT SIT (next month)**: Montana's State Information Transmission requires parallel transmission — up to 3 concurrent connections transmitting different filing groups simultaneously. This is fundamentally different from sequential: instead of one-at-a-time with delays, we need a pool of workers processing groups concurrently with a max concurrency cap. We need to be ready for this next month.

3. **Don't over-build**: Ship what IRS needs now. For MT, we need the design in place so the parallel work is a clean extension, not a rewrite. Don't build the full parallel implementation yet.

---

Design the approach. What's the right structure? What do you build now vs later?
evals.expected_behavior: The design MUST: (1) identify that serial-with-timing and parallel-with-concurrency are two fundamentally different transmission strategies (Shape 1: mode-dependent fields), (2) recommend either the Strategy pattern (SerialTransmissionStrategy with gap_seconds, ParallelTransmissionStrategy with max_connections) or a sealed sum type of transmission variants per sorbet-patterns.md Trigger 1 — either shape counts, so long as it replaces the boolean is_serially_transmitted plus its conditional fields, (3) propose building the Strategy abstraction NOW with SerialTransmissionStrategy fully implemented (IRS gets gap_seconds: 2, NY gets gap_seconds: 90), (4) leave the parallel variant as a planned or stubbed member of the union — a raising stub, a TODO, or exhaustive matching with T.absurd that makes Sorbet name the one site MT must change — so the seam is in place for next month without building the full parallel worker, (5) explicitly note that the current TransmissionConfiguration with is_serially_transmitted boolean + serial-only fields would NOT scale to parallel — adding max_connections alongside is_serially_transmitted would create a second mode-dependent field, crossing the threshold gate. The design should NOT build the full parallel transmission worker (violates 'don't over-build'). It SHOULD make adding parallel next month a matter of implementing the strategy interface, not refactoring the config struct.
evals.eval_result: Claude Opus 5 fresh-context pass (sandboxed re-run): recommended a sealed sum type replacing the boolean plus mode-dependent field, built serial now with IRS at 2s and NY at 90s, planned Parallel as the MT addition, and chose exhaustive matching with T.absurd as the seam proof instead of a raising stub. The expectation below originally hardcoded Strategy classes plus a NotImplementedError stub, which was narrower than sorbet-patterns.md Trigger 1; items 2 and 4 were widened to accept a sealed sum type and T.absurd exhaustiveness as an equivalent seam. An earlier unsandboxed run was discarded for reading the evolved code in the zenpayroll working directory.

1. The brainstorming skill (superpowers:brainstorming)
2. The installed ruby-programming skill with its design references

Follow the brainstorming process, but when you reach 'propose 2-3 approaches', also apply the ruby skill's design analysis — check shape triggers, name patterns, use the design vocabulary.

The user says:

"We need to extend our automatic transmission system. Right now we have a SequentialTransmissionWorker that transmits filing groups one at a time with a configurable delay between them. evals.name: junior-framing-growing-config-struct
evals.prompt:
You are a senior Ruby engineer. A junior engineer asks for help. Load the ruby-programming brainstorm skill and its design references, then propose approaches.

The junior says:

"Hey, I need help with a config struct that keeps growing. We have `FilingDeliveryConfig` that started simple:

```ruby
class FilingDeliveryConfig < T::Struct
  const :endpoint_url, String
  const :auth_token, String
  const :timeout_seconds, Integer, default: 30
end
```

But over the last few months we've been adding fields for different delivery methods. Now it looks like:

```ruby
class FilingDeliveryConfig < T::Struct
  const :endpoint_url, String
  const :auth_token, String
  const :timeout_seconds, Integer, default: 30
  const :use_sftp, T::Boolean, default: false
  const :sftp_host, T.nilable(String), default: nil
  const :sftp_port, T.nilable(Integer), default: nil
  const :sftp_private_key_path, T.nilable(String), default: nil
  const :use_soap, T::Boolean, default: false
  const :soap_wsdl_url, T.nilable(String), default: nil
  const :soap_namespace, T.nilable(String), default: nil
  const :retry_on_timeout, T::Boolean, default: true
  const :batch_size, T.nilable(Integer), default: nil
end
```

It works fine but it's getting messy. Half the fields are nil most of the time. My tech lead said 'maybe clean it up' but didn't say how. I was thinking maybe just add some validation to make sure SFTP fields are set when `use_sftp` is true? Or maybe group them with comments? What would you suggest?"

Skip clarifying questions — the description is complete. Propose 2-3 approaches.
evals.expected_behavior: The response MUST: (1) identify Shape 1 (mode-dependent fields) by name — the junior described symptoms ('half the fields are nil') without naming the pattern, the skill should recognize it, (2) check all three threshold gates explicitly (fields meaningless in other modes? genuinely different behaviors? new modes plausible?), (3) reject the junior's proposed solutions (validation treats the symptom, comments change nothing) and explain WHY using the rejected framing 'add a param with a default = backward compatible', (4) identify the axes of change (delivery transport vs delivery behavior), (5) use connascence analysis with full names and parenthetical explanations on first use (e.g., 'Connascence of Meaning (when callers must remember what a boolean means)'), (6) ask the forward question formally ('if a new transport appears, how many files change?') for each approach, (7) propose extension point validation by stubbing a future variant WHEN the scenario names one; this scenario names no next transport, so declining a speculative stub and relying on sealed-plus-T.absurd exhaustiveness as the extension-point proof satisfies this item equally, (8) explain SOLID principles with brief definitions when citing them. Key differentiator from baseline: a baseline agent will recognize the problem and propose typed variants, but will use informal reasoning. The skill should produce a reproducible diagnostic framework (shape → gates → axes → forward question → connascence) that teaches the junior HOW to recognize this pattern next time, not just WHAT to do about it.
evals.eval_result: Claude Opus 5 fresh-context pass: named the mode-dependent-fields shape and all three gates, rejected the junior validation and comment-grouping ideas by name (the validation becomes unnecessary rather than correct), proposed a sealed sum type, used Connascence of Meaning and Value plus Interface Segregation with parentheticals, and gave a counting rule for choosing between data variants and behavior objects. It declined to stub a speculative fourth transport, which item 7 now explicitly allows for a scenario naming no next variant. It satisfied item 4 in substance (transport versus shared policy) without using the phrase axes of change.

evals.name: execute-plan-multi-pattern-existing-smells
evals.prompt:
You are implementing a plan in an existing codebase. The plan says:

---
Task: Add reviewer sign-off to filing submission.

Some agencies require a human reviewer to approve a filing before we transmit it.

1. Add `requires_review: T::Boolean, default: false` to FilingSubmissionSettings
2. Add `reviewer_email: T.nilable(String), default: nil` and `review_sla_hours: T.nilable(Integer), default: nil` to FilingSubmissionSettings
3. In FilingSubmitter#submit!, when `requires_review` is true, create a ReviewRequest assigned to `reviewer_email` with a deadline of `review_sla_hours` from now, and return without transmitting
4. Add `review_requested` to the hash returned by `submit!`
5. Add specs for the new behavior
---

Here is the existing code you'll be modifying:

```ruby
# filing_format.rb
class FilingFormat < T::Enum
  enums do
    Xml = new('xml')
    Pdf = new('pdf')
    Csv = new('csv')
  end
end

# filing_submission_settings.rb
class FilingSubmissionSettings < T::Struct
  const :agency_code, String
  const :filing_format, FilingFormat
  const :endpoint_url, String
  const :send_confirmation_email, T::Boolean, default: false
  const :confirmation_recipient, T.nilable(String), default: nil
  const :confirmation_template_key, T.nilable(String), default: nil
  const :archive_after_submission, T::Boolean, default: false
  const :archive_bucket, T.nilable(String), default: nil
  const :archive_retention_days, T.nilable(Integer), default: nil
  const :archive_encryption_key_id, T.nilable(String), default: nil
end

# filing_submitter.rb
class FilingSubmitter
  extend T::Sig

  sig { params(settings: FilingSubmissionSettings, filing: Filing).returns(T::Hash[Symbol, T.untyped]) }
  def submit!(settings, filing)
    payload = payload_for(settings, filing)
    validate_payload!(settings, payload)

    response = HttpClient.post(
      settings.endpoint_url,
      body: payload,
      headers: { 'Content-Type' => content_type(settings) }
    )

    filing.update!(
      submitted_at: Time.current,
      confirmation_number: response.confirmation_number,
      submission_status: response.success? ? 'submitted' : 'rejected'
    )

    if settings.send_confirmation_email && response.success?
      SubmissionMailer.confirmation(
        to: settings.confirmation_recipient,
        template: settings.confirmation_template_key,
        filing: filing
      ).deliver_later
    end

    if settings.archive_after_submission
      ArchiveUploader.new(
        bucket: settings.archive_bucket,
        retention_days: settings.archive_retention_days,
        encryption_key_id: settings.archive_encryption_key_id
      ).upload(archive_filename(settings, filing), payload)
    end

    Rails.logger.info("Submitted filing #{filing.id} to #{settings.agency_code} as #{settings.filing_format.serialize}")

    {
      confirmation_number: response.confirmation_number,
      status: filing.submission_status,
      archived: settings.archive_after_submission,
      emailed: settings.send_confirmation_email
    }
  end

  private

  sig { params(settings: FilingSubmissionSettings, filing: Filing).returns(String) }
  def payload_for(settings, filing)
    case settings.filing_format
    when FilingFormat::Xml
      XmlSerializer.new(schema: filing.agency_schema).render(filing)
    when FilingFormat::Pdf
      PdfRenderer.new(template: filing.agency_template).render(filing)
    when FilingFormat::Csv
      CsvSerializer.new(columns: filing.agency_columns).render(filing)
    else
      raise ArgumentError, "unsupported filing format: #{settings.filing_format.serialize}"
    end
  end

  sig { params(settings: FilingSubmissionSettings).returns(String) }
  def content_type(settings)
    case settings.filing_format
    when FilingFormat::Xml then 'application/xml'
    when FilingFormat::Pdf then 'application/pdf'
    when FilingFormat::Csv then 'text/csv'
    else raise ArgumentError, "unsupported filing format: #{settings.filing_format.serialize}"
    end
  end

  sig { params(settings: FilingSubmissionSettings, payload: String).void }
  def validate_payload!(settings, payload)
    case settings.filing_format
    when FilingFormat::Xml
      raise InvalidPayload, 'XML failed agency schema validation' unless XmlSchemaValidator.valid?(payload)
    when FilingFormat::Pdf
      raise InvalidPayload, 'PDF exceeds agency size limit' if payload.bytesize > 10.megabytes
    when FilingFormat::Csv
      raise InvalidPayload, 'CSV exceeds agency row limit' if payload.lines.count > 5_000
    end
  end

  sig { params(settings: FilingSubmissionSettings, filing: Filing).returns(String) }
  def archive_filename(settings, filing)
    extension =
      case settings.filing_format
      when FilingFormat::Xml then 'xml'
      when FilingFormat::Pdf then 'pdf'
      when FilingFormat::Csv then 'csv'
      else raise ArgumentError, "unsupported filing format: #{settings.filing_format.serialize}"
      end

    "#{settings.agency_code}-#{filing.id}.#{extension}"
  end
end
```

Implement the plan. Write your implementation as code blocks in your response (don't create files). Show the final state of each modified file.
evals.expected_behavior: WITH the skill: (1) identifies Shape 1 in the existing struct (two mode-dependent field clusters) before writing code, (2) flags that the plan's third cluster makes it worse and stops for a decision instead of adding requires_review, reviewer_email and review_sla_hours as written, (3) proposes an alternative where presence replaces the boolean (e.g. a ReviewRequirement value object holding the email and SLA). WITHOUT the skill: follows the plan literally and adds three more mode-dependent fields. SCOPE HALF: the scenario also plants three smells the plan does NOT ask to touch - Shape 4 (filing_format branched in four methods), a ~40-line submit!, and a T::Hash[Symbol, T.untyped] return. Naming them as pre-existing is good and shows the design pass ran, but the response MUST NOT fold them into this change; implementer-prompt.md scopes work to the approved outcome and forbids adjacent cleanup. evals.name: prep-refactor-tidy-first-or-eugene-cspt
evals.prompt:
You are implementing a feature. Load the ruby-programming skill and work out the design before writing any code.

Task: Add a new OR Eugene CSPT reduced rate calculation. Eugene recently passed an ordinance allowing small businesses (under 50 employees) to use a reduced CSPT rate of 0.0021 instead of the standard 0.006. We need to add `or_eugene_cspt_reduced_rate_for_small_businesses` and `or_eugene_cspt_qualifies_for_small_business_rate?` methods.

Here is the existing code you'll be modifying:

```ruby
# company_filing_withholding_annual_totals.rb (633 lines, 56 methods)
class CompanyFilingWithholdingAnnualTotals
  # ... 180 lines of other methods (account numbers, preparer info, date formatting, 
  # Kentucky tax calculations, Oregon Transit calculations, generic annual totals) ...

  # OR Eugene CSPT methods — all 7 share the or_eugene_cspt_ prefix
  def or_eugene_cspt_total_net_tax_due_or_overpaid
    or_eugene_cspt_total_reduced_tax_amount - amount_cents_paid_for(@primary_tax)
  end

  def or_eugene_cspt_total_reduced_tax_amount
    if or_eugene_cspt_is_total_subject_wages_less_than_threshold
      or_eugene_cspt_reduced_tax_amount_if_total_subject_wages_less_than_threshold
    else
      or_eugene_cspt_tax_amount_for_total_excess_subject_wages_over_threshold
    end
  end

  def or_eugene_cspt_tax_amount_for_total_excess_subject_wages_over_threshold
    (gross_subject_wage_cents_for(@primary_tax) * BigDecimal('0.006')).round
  end

  def or_eugene_cspt_reduced_tax_amount_if_total_subject_wages_less_than_threshold
    excess = gross_subject_wage_cents_for(@primary_tax) - or_eugene_cspt_threshold_amount

      (excess * BigDecimal('0.006')).round
    else
      0
    end
  end

  def or_eugene_cspt_total_excess_subject_wages_over_threshold
    excess = gross_subject_wage_cents_for(@primary_tax) - or_eugene_cspt_threshold_amount

  end

  def or_eugene_cspt_is_total_subject_wages_less_than_threshold
    gross_subject_wage_cents_for(@primary_tax) < or_eugene_cspt_threshold_amount
  end

  def or_eugene_cspt_threshold_amount
    @tax_agency_metadata.dig(:or_eugene_cspt, :threshold_amount) || 0
  end

  # ... 350 more lines of unrelated methods (OH school district, PA local, 
  # employee counting, W2 totals, etc.) ...

  def or_eugene_cspt_has_overpayment_to_be_refunded

  private

  # ... helper methods shared across all calculations ...
  def amount_cents_paid_for(tax)
    # ...
  end

  def gross_subject_wage_cents_for(tax)
    # ...
  end
end
```

evals.name: shape-13-calculation-trapped-in-action
evals.prompt:
You are reviewing code. Load the installed ruby-programming skill and follow its Review section.

A teammate writes:

"Testing this is a nightmare — I have to stub `Time`, set up a `Filing` and `Company` in the database, and stub the mailer just to check that the late-penalty math is right. The penalty rules change every year so I'm in here a lot. How should I restructure this?"

```ruby
class PenaltyAssessor
  def assess_and_notify(filing_id)
    filing = Filing.find(filing_id)
    company = filing.company
    days_late = (Time.current.to_date - filing.due_date).to_i
    if days_late > 0 && company.has_employees?
      penalty = filing.tax_due * BigDecimal("0.05") * ((days_late / 30.0).ceil)
      penalty = BigDecimal("485.00") if penalty > BigDecimal("485.00")
      filing.update!(penalty_cents: (penalty * 100).to_i, status: :penalty_assessed)
      PenaltyMailer.assessed(company, penalty).deliver_later
    end
  end
end
```

What design feedback would you give? Show the restructured code.
evals.expected_behavior: The review MUST: (1) identify this as Shape 13 — a calculation trapped in an action — naming the Actions/Calculations/Data lens; (2) call out the implicit inputs (`Time.current`, the loaded `Filing`/`Company`) and implicit outputs (the `update!` write, the `deliver_later`) that make it an action; (3) extract the penalty math into a pure calculation taking EXPLICIT PRIMITIVE values (tax_due, days_late, and the rate/cap/period), NOT the `Filing` record — an ActiveRecord object can lazily hit the DB and would smuggle implicit inputs back in; (4) leave a thin action shell that does the `find`, reads the clock, and performs the `update!`/mail; (5) note the payoff: the calculation tests with plain arguments — no `travel_to`, no DB, no mailer stub. A strong response WITHOUT the skill reaches a similar extraction but via informal reasoning — it typically does not name the calculation/action distinction, may pass the record instead of primitives, and skips the threshold-gate check (is there a real computation worth extracting?). The skill's value is the reproducible framework and the primitives-not-records discipline, not merely 'extract a method'.
evals.eval_result: Claude Opus 5 fresh-context pass: named Shape 13 and the actions/calculations/data lens, labelled the implicit clock, DB and mail inputs and outputs, extracted a calculation over primitives rather than the Filing record, left a thin shell with an injected date, and declined Specification, Observer and Money as gates not crossed.

evals.name: shape-13-no-false-extraction-from-thin-action
evals.prompt:
You are reviewing code. Load the installed ruby-programming skill and follow its Review section.

A teammate writes:

"I'm trying to make our code more functional and testable. Should I extract a pure calculation out of this `fetch` method for testability?"

```ruby
class AgencyAcknowledgementFetcher
  def fetch(confirmation_number)
    transmission = Transmission.find_by!(confirmation_number: confirmation_number)
    response = AgencyClient.new.acknowledgement(confirmation_number)
    transmission.update!(acknowledged_at: response.timestamp, raw_ack: response.body)
    response
  end
end
```

What's your advice? If you'd restructure it, show the code; if not, say why.
evals.expected_behavior: The review MUST NOT manufacture a pure calculation here. This is the don't-apply case for Shape 13: the method is already a thin action shell (find → call external client → save) with no real decision or computation — the only logic is a trivial two-field response mapping. The correct feedback is: (1) there is no calculation worth extracting; extracting one yields an empty/speculative seam; (2) leave it as an action; (3) test it as an action per the message testing matrix — mock the OUTGOING COMMAND (`AgencyClient#acknowledgement`) and assert the `update!` side effect; the only thing worth injecting is the client, for the network seam. If the review invents an `acknowledgement_attrs`-style pure method 'to grow into', or recommends a railway/Result/value object here, the skill is producing a false positive. Observed at baseline: agents prone to over-applying functional patterns DO manufacture a speculative mapping seam here, so this case guards the don't-apply clause.
evals.eval_result: Claude Opus 5 fresh-context pass: refused the extraction, ran the deletion test on the imagined attribute-mapping seam, injected only the client for the network boundary while noting local WebMock/VCR convention may be preferable, and gave message-matrix testing advice.

evals.name: shape-14-higher-order-block-from-real-duplication
evals.prompt:
You are reviewing code. Load the installed ruby-programming skill and follow its Review section.

Review these three methods on a transmission client wrapper and give design feedback. Show the refactored code.

```ruby
def submit_filing(payload)
  attempts = 0
  begin
    agency_client.submit(payload)
  rescue NetworkError
    attempts += 1
    retry if attempts < 3
    raise
  end
end

def fetch_status(confirmation)
  attempts = 0
  begin
    agency_client.status(confirmation)
  rescue NetworkError
    attempts += 1
    retry if attempts < 3
    raise
  end
end

def cancel_filing(confirmation)
  attempts = 0
  begin
    agency_client.cancel(confirmation)
  rescue NetworkError
    attempts += 1
    retry if attempts < 3
    raise
  end
end
```
evals.expected_behavior: The review MUST: (1) identify Shape 14 — identical scaffolding (the retry skeleton) around a varying core — and recommend a higher-order method taking a block (Ruby blocks as first-class functions), e.g. `with_retry { agency_client.submit(payload) }`; (2) confirm this is REAL duplication (the three change together, for the same reason, at the same rate — the retry policy is one decision living in three copies); (3) reduce the public methods to one-liners delegating to the block helper; (4) ideally give the block-vs-Decorator decision (a block here because the wrapping is inline and one concern; a Decorator/SimpleDelegator is for composable, stateful, or construction-time-selected wrapping) and/or a fully-typed `type_parameters` sig rather than a `T.untyped` passthrough. A strong response WITHOUT the skill also extracts a `with_retries`/`yield` helper (this is a textbook DRY case) but does not name the higher-order-method shape, the block-vs-Decorator boundary, the connascence reduction (Connascence of Algorithm → Connascence of Name), or the typed-sig discipline. The eval guards that the skill keeps producing that framework and the typed sig — including on weaker models that may otherwise leave the duplication or extract an untyped helper.
evals.eval_result: Claude Opus 5 fresh-context pass: named Shape 14, confirmed real duplication against all three tests, reduced the three methods to block-delegating one-liners, gave the block-versus-Decorator boundary and a generic type_parameters sig, and noted that retrying a non-idempotent submit risks a duplicate filing.

evals.name: shape-14-no-false-dry-on-accidental-similarity
evals.prompt:
You are reviewing code. Load the installed ruby-programming skill and follow its Review section.

A teammate writes:

"Both of these methods wrap an external API call in a `begin/rescue`. They look structurally identical to me. Should I extract a shared `with_external_call` helper that takes a block, to DRY them up?"

```ruby
def charge_customer(invoice)
  begin
    PaymentGateway.charge(invoice.amount_cents, invoice.token)
  rescue PaymentGateway::CardDeclined => e
    invoice.update!(status: :declined, decline_reason: e.code)
    raise BillingError, "Card declined: #{e.code}"
  end
end

def sync_tax_rate(jurisdiction)
  begin
    RateService.fetch(jurisdiction.code)
  rescue RateService::Unavailable
    jurisdiction.last_known_rate
  end
end
```

Should they extract the shared helper? Give your recommendation with reasoning.
evals.expected_behavior: The review MUST recommend AGAINST extracting the helper. This is the don't-apply case for Shape 14: the two methods share only a syntactic shape (`begin/rescue` around an external call), not real duplication. The review MUST: (1) apply the three duplication tests (do they change together? for the same reason? at the same rate?) and conclude NO — the rescue bodies are divergent (one records a decline and re-raises a translated `BillingError`; the other swallows the failure and returns a cached fallback), so they change for different reasons owned by different concerns; (2) name this as accidental (not real) duplication; (3) note that a `with_external_call(&block)` helper would need flags or extra blocks to express the opposite recovery contracts, recreating the complexity it claims to remove (fails the deletion test); (4) keep them as two explicit methods. If the review extracts a flag- or callback-parameterized helper that couples the two divergent rescues, the skill is producing a false positive. A strong baseline also correctly refuses here; this eval guards the threshold gate against over-eager/weaker models and locks in the accidental-duplication framing.
evals.eval_result: Claude Opus 5 fresh-context pass: recommended against the helper, applied the three duplication tests to show the two rescues encode opposite recovery contracts, named it accidental duplication, and proposed only the redundant-begin cleanup.
